name: National church established
description: The English Reformation established the Church of England as a national church.
narrative: The English Reformation established the Church of England as a national church. The Reformation separated English church authority from Rome through royal and parliamentary action. Subsequent settlements established a distinctive combination of Reformed teaching, common prayer, and historic episcopal ministry. The church’s own doctrinal canons identify Scripture, the Articles, prayer book, and Ordinal as guiding sources. Its members have differed substantially in churchmanship, and the 1534 marker should be explained as a jurisdictional break rather than the beginning of Christianity in England.

key_figures.name: Thomas Cranmer
key_figures.summary: The English archbishop whose liturgical work helped make common prayer a central expression of reformed English Christianity.

key_figures.name: Henry VIII
key_figures.role: political agent of separation from Rome, not author of the later entire doctrinal settlement
key_figures.summary: The English monarch whose marital and jurisdictional conflict with Rome led to royal supremacy; his political break did not immediately settle all later Protestant doctrine.

name: American church formed
description: The Episcopal Church formed as the U.S. Anglican body after separation from the Church of England.
narrative: The Episcopal Church formed as the U.S. Anglican body after separation from the Church of England. American independence made dependence on English royal and ecclesiastical structures impractical. Clergy and lay representatives developed conventions and a constitution while securing a local episcopate. The first General Convention in 1785 and the prayer-book and constitutional settlement of 1789 are distinct milestones. The resulting church continued Anglican worship while adapting governance to an American setting; later conflicts did not end the parent church.
